chapters.applicability: General thermoplastic reciprocating-screw moulding. Transfer methods and signal quality depend on the machine, mould and instrumentation.

sections.title: Transfer is a control transition, not a universal percentage
sections.text: Transfer is the point at which the control strategy changes from filling the cavity to holding pressure while the part packs and cools. It is not automatically a fixed percentage or a universal position. If transfer occurs too early or too late for a particular process, the evidence may include fill progression, cushion, pressure traces, part weight, flash or dimensional response. First learn what the machine’s transfer signal represents; then compare repeatable cycles and parts. Any adjustment belongs to an approved process-development study, not a generic percentage rule.

sections.title: Look for evidence of early or late transfer
sections.text: A transfer that occurs too early for the actual process can leave the cavity dependent on post-transfer filling, while a transfer that occurs too late can create excessive pressure response or overfill tendencies. Interpret the evidence as a pattern across position, pressure, time, cavity behaviour and part results rather than declaring one trace feature to be proof by itself.

sections.title: Judge transfer by repeatability and downstream response
sections.text: A useful transfer method should produce a repeatable transition under the actual material, machine and mould conditions. Compare the trigger, cavity or machine pressure response, part mass and key dimensions across repeated cycles and normal operating variation. A transfer point that looks acceptable in one trace but shifts product response from cycle to cycle is not yet a robust basis for production.

sections.title: Worked example (hypothetical): separate transfer evidence from a local flash symptom
sections.text:
Imagine two study runs use the same requested transfer point, but the part results differ: one run has a thin region in one cavity and a small flash mark near a different cavity. It is tempting to call both outcomes a transfer problem. Begin by describing them separately. Record which cavity shows each symptom, whether the pattern repeats, and when each change appears in the cycle.

Place the available evidence on one timeline: commanded filling profile, achieved screw motion, the transfer event, any pressure signal, clamp response if measured, and the part observations. Ask whether the difference starts before transfer, around the transition, or later in the post-fill period. If the fill pattern already differs before the transition, the transfer point alone cannot explain the first divergence. If filling looks comparable but the response separates after transfer, investigate how the post-fill state is delivered and observed. If flash remains fixed to one local feature, inspect mould support, shutoff condition and contamination through the approved tooling route.

Each hypothesis predicts a different pattern. A transition-related explanation should fit the timing and downstream response. A local tooling explanation should fit the position of the flash. A single machine display cannot prove either one. Keep the two observations separate until the evidence connects them.

A useful record states what was commanded, what the machine actually did, where the cavity or mould evidence came from, and which part characteristic changed. It also names missing measurements. The example does not prescribe a transfer trigger or clamp setting; it shows how to avoid changing both at once and then losing the ability to learn from the result.

The clamp question needs its own evidence. If a flash mark appears, compare its location and onset with the transfer and pressure history, then consider parting-line support and mould condition. A transfer point that repeats does not establish that local pressure or mould support is adequate. Likewise, one flash mark does not establish that the clamp system is generally undersized. The two symptoms may share a process condition, or they may need separate investigations. Keeping them separate prevents a global control change from being used to hide a local tooling issue.

chapters.applicability: Conceptual relationship only. Required clamp capability depends on projected area, cavity pressure distribution, mould construction and machine limits.

sections.title: What clamp force resists
sections.text: Clamp force resists the pressure-driven tendency for the mould halves to separate, but the demand is distributed over the projected area exposed to cavity pressure. The pressure is not uniform everywhere, so nominal tonnage alone cannot diagnose a local flash mark. Mould support, alignment, parting-line condition, local pressure, material response and machine behaviour all affect the result. Learn the difference between mould protection and production clamp force, and never treat increasing force as an unlimited corrective action. Inspect and measure through authorised procedures.

sections.title: Mould protection is different
sections.text: Low-force mould-protection functions are intended to detect abnormal resistance during closing; they are not a substitute for correct tooling, guarding, maintenance or the machine manufacturer's setup procedure.

sections.title: Clamp demand is a distributed-pressure problem
sections.text: The mould-opening tendency depends on pressure acting over projected areas, but cavity pressure is not uniform in space or time and machine injection pressure is not a direct substitute for the pressure distribution at the parting line. Clamp calculations are therefore engineering estimates whose assumptions should be visible. They can support machine and process decisions, but they do not automatically define the required machine rating.

sections.title: Flash is not automatically a clamp-tonnage diagnosis
sections.text: Flash can involve clamp force, pressure, mould damage, parting-line contamination, local support, temperature, viscosity, vent geometry or other mechanisms. Increasing clamp force without evidence can hide tooling issues or move the process toward equipment limits. Check where flash occurs, whether it is cavity-specific, how it changes with pressure history and whether the mould closes and supports correctly before naming the cause.

sections.title: Use clamp evidence with mould condition evidence
sections.text: Clamp demand cannot be separated completely from the mould's mechanical condition. Parting-line damage, support, contamination, thermal growth and local shutoff geometry can alter where opening or flash occurs. A useful investigation combines the pressure/projected-area estimate with inspection and location evidence so that a tooling problem is not mislabelled as insufficient machine tonnage.

chapters.applicability: General cold- and hot-feed-system concepts; actual dimensions and limits are mould-specific.

sections.title: Flow path
sections.text: The feed system carries melt from the machine nozzle through the sprue and runners to the gate. Every change in channel size, length, surface, junction or temperature affects the pressure and thermal history needed to move material. A cavity may therefore fill differently even when the machine command is unchanged. Follow the path from nozzle to gate and use the observed cavity pattern to locate where differences begin. Tool changes or hot-runner interventions require qualified review of the specific mould and system documentation.

sections.title: Gates are process boundaries
sections.text: Gate geometry controls how the cavity is fed and how long post-fill pressure can influence the part. Changing a gate can alter filling, packing, orientation and appearance together.

sections.title: Diagnose by location
sections.text: When a restriction is suspected, separate machine/nozzle, sprue, runner, gate and cavity contributions using measured or controlled comparisons instead of assuming the smallest feature is automatically the root cause.

sections.title: Balance pressure loss against thermal and shear history
sections.text: A restriction changes more than the pressure required to fill. It can also alter shear, local heating, residence and the sensitivity of downstream filling to small changes in material condition. When comparing feed-system sections, record the pressure change together with fill behaviour and part response so that a high pressure drop is interpreted in its physical context rather than treated as a defect by itself.

chapters.applicability: General mechanism guidance. Vent geometry, cleaning and permissible modification are mould- and material-specific.

sections.title: Air must leave
sections.text: As melt enters a cavity, it displaces air and other gases. Vents provide an escape path, but vent performance depends on location, cleanliness, geometry and how the flow front approaches the feature. A burn mark at end of fill can fit trapped gas, yet a similar mark can also arise from degraded material or contamination. Map where the mark appears and whether it follows a cavity, flow-front or material pattern. Vent cleaning or steel changes are tooling work governed by the mould drawing and authorised maintenance process.

sections.title: Burns are not one mechanism
sections.text: A dark mark near an end-of-fill region can be consistent with compressed gas, but thermal degradation, contamination and excessive residence history can produce similar evidence.

sections.title: Test before changing steel
sections.text: Use defect location, fill progression, vent condition and controlled process changes to test the hypothesis. Permanent vent changes require tooling authority and mould-specific limits.

sections.title: Use the defect location to test the gas hypothesis
sections.text: A gas-related mechanism should make predictions about where air is trapped or forced to escape. Compare end-of-fill locations, converging flow fronts, ribs, blind pockets and vent condition with the mark or fill disturbance. If the defect moves independently of those boundaries, broaden the investigation to degradation, contamination or other mechanisms instead of assuming venting is always responsible.

chapters.applicability: Heat-transfer principles only. Coolant, flow, pressure, mould materials and allowable temperatures are tool- and site-specific.

sections.title: Cooling governs both cycle readiness and dimensional state
sections.text: Cooling removes heat until the part is sufficiently stable for the next stage and release. The controller’s coolant setpoint is not the same as the mould’s actual temperature field, and a single outlet reading cannot describe every cavity or channel. Flow, deposits, leaks, contact, wall thickness and channel layout can all affect heat removal. Compare equivalent cycles, cavity locations and measurements; then relate thermal evidence to cycle time, ejection and dimensions. Cooling changes can alter several outcomes at once, so record the process and part response.

sections.title: Diagnose the thermal system with trends, not one reading
sections.text: Useful evidence can include coolant supply and return conditions, mould-surface measurements, cycle-to-cycle warm-up behaviour, cavity pattern, part temperature and dimensional change after ejection. A single temperature measurement may miss an imbalance. Look for spatial and time patterns that distinguish a stable offset from changing heat load, restricted flow, poor contact or another thermal mechanism.

sections.title: Thermal gradients can create dimensional gradients
sections.text: Different regions can stiffen and contract at different rates. Thick sections, isolated cores, deep ribs or poorly balanced cooling can therefore leave different parts of the moulding at different temperatures and stress states when ejection occurs. Those differences can later appear as warpage, local shrinkage or changing dimensions.

sections.title: Compare equivalent thermal states
sections.text: A start-up part, a part from a thermally stable mould and a part made after an interruption may not be comparable even when machine setpoints are unchanged. Track cycle count or stable-state evidence where relevant so that thermal drift is not mistaken for a direct effect of another process variable.

sections.title: When cooling stops fitting the evidence
sections.text: Reconsider cooling as the leading mechanism when the defect does not track thermal stabilisation, measured temperature patterns, cavity location or changes that should alter heat removal. Persistent local effects may instead point toward geometry, pressure transmission, material anisotropy or tooling condition.

chapters.applicability: General release mechanisms. Draft requirements and ejection limits depend on geometry, texture, material and tool construction.

sections.title: Release force carries information
sections.text: Ejection is the final handoff from moulded geometry to the outside world. Draft, surface texture, undercuts, core layout, ejector support and the part’s local shrinkage influence how easily it releases. High release force may reflect the mould, but distortion can also be created earlier by cooling or packing and only become visible during ejection. Record the exact location and direction of witness marks, drag or deformation, and compare cavities and equivalent parts. Any tooling or ejection adjustment must be assessed against the approved mould design and safety procedure.

sections.title: Separate geometry from process effects
sections.text: If a release problem follows one feature or cavity consistently, geometry, finish, venting or local cooling deserves attention. If it drifts with mould temperature or cycle state, process and thermal mechanisms become more plausible. Controlled comparisons help avoid using process compensation to mask a tooling condition that requires inspection or repair.

sections.title: Separate sticking from distortion caused before release
sections.text: A distorted part at ejection can reflect high release load, but it can also carry residual stress or thermal non-uniformity created earlier in the cycle. Observe whether marks align with ejector locations, draw direction, texture, undercuts or local hot regions before attributing every post-ejection shape change to the ejection system itself.

sections.title: Use the location of witness and drag evidence
sections.text: Whitening, scuffing, pin witness or drag marks provide spatial information. A local mark near a textured or low-draft feature supports a different mechanism from widespread deformation on a still-hot part. Map these observations to the physical tooling before changing process conditions.

sections.title: Cooling and pressure history can alter release load
sections.text: Part stiffness at ejection and contraction onto cores are influenced by thermal state and the way the part was packed and cooled. Process changes can therefore alter release behaviour even when the tool is unchanged. That does not mean a mechanical interference, damaged surface or inadequate draft should be compensated indefinitely with process settings.

sections.title: Tooling evidence should trigger tooling action
sections.text: Repeated evidence of mechanical interference, damaged shutoffs, rough surfaces, undercut or insufficient draft should be escalated as a tooling/design condition. The process should not be driven toward unstable or unsafe limits simply to make a mechanically constrained part leave the mould.

sections.title: Signals that point away from a release-only explanation
sections.text: Change the diagnosis when the mark does not follow the expected tooling feature, when extra cooling changes distortion but not drag, or when inspection identifies a physical interference. Treat symptom improvement as provisional until the mechanical and thermal evidence agree.

sections.title: Worked example (hypothetical): a part distorts while leaving one core
sections.text:
A part from one cavity shows a local drag mark and a bent feature after ejection. A beginner may assume that ejection force caused the whole distortion. Treat the mark and the shape change as related observations, not proof of one cause.

Start with location. Does the drag mark follow an ejector, a textured face, an undercut or a particular core surface? Is the bend near that location, or elsewhere in the part? Record whether the symptom occurs in the same cavity and whether the part is still warm or changes shape after release. These observations help separate a local release interaction from deformation that developed earlier through uneven cooling, contraction or residual stress.

Then compare the actual evidence that could distinguish the mechanisms: cavity identity, mark position, part temperature or another approved thermal measure, ejection timing and the part's shape before and after release. Tool inspection may be needed to evaluate draft, surface condition, damage, contamination or alignment. Follow the machine and tooling procedures for any inspection or intervention.

If the mark is fixed to one feature while the broader distortion changes with thermal state, the investigation may involve both a local tooling condition and a process-related part condition. Do not respond by increasing ejection force or cooling time automatically. Either change could alter the symptom without identifying its source. Record which evidence supports sticking, which supports pre-ejection deformation, and what remains unknown. The example is a reasoning exercise, not an ejection setting or repair instruction.

chapters.applicability: General hot-runner concepts only. Temperatures, start-up, shutdown, maintenance and valve-gate timing must follow the installed supplier's documentation.

sections.title: A heated feed system is part of the process
sections.text: A hot runner keeps part of the feed system heated so that material can remain molten between the machine and cavity. Each zone becomes part of the polymer’s temperature and residence-time history. A controller setpoint is not proof that the manifold, nozzle or gate has the intended thermal condition; a sensor can be offset or a zone can respond differently. Identify which circuit and location a signal represents, then compare startup, steady-state and interruption history with the exact system manual. Hot-runner work is system-specific.

sections.title: Thermal history can differ by location
sections.text: Manifold and nozzle temperatures, residence distribution and local restrictions can affect viscosity and degradation risk. A controller setpoint alone does not prove melt condition.

sections.title: Supplier instructions control
sections.text: Start-up, shutdown, purge, heater limits, valve-gate operation and maintenance are hardware- and material-dependent. Generic Book guidance cannot safely replace the hot-runner supplier's procedure.

sections.title: Treat each heated zone as part of the material history
sections.text: A hot-runner system can create different residence and thermal conditions across manifolds, drops and valve-gate regions. A common controller setpoint does not prove identical melt history at every location. Cavity-specific defects, colour change, pressure imbalance or restart behaviour can therefore provide clues about where the heated feed system deserves inspection or supplier-guided diagnosis.

sections.title: Worked example (hypothetical): a colour mark after a production interruption
sections.text:
Suppose a colour mark appears during the first stable-looking cycles after an interruption. The controller still displays its previous hot-runner zone setpoints, and the mark appears in parts from only one cavity. Those facts are useful, but neither proves that a heater zone caused the mark. A displayed setpoint is not a measurement of every local melt condition, and the visual defect is not a unique diagnosis.

First map the mark by cavity and by its position within each part. Then put the event on a timeline: last known-good parts, interruption, restart, the first affected cycle, and any later recovery or recurrence. Compare that timing with the material changeover or residence history and with the hot-runner system's documented restart state. The installed supplier's instructions control restart, purge, heater limits and valve-gate operation; this example does not add a procedure.

If the same cavity and local region recur, a local drop, gate or mould condition becomes a question to investigate alongside thermal history. If several cavities show the same change at the same time, a shared material, machine or system condition deserves attention. If the mark follows a material container or colour transition instead of a cavity, the material path is another boundary. These patterns rank questions; they do not identify a root cause on their own.

A useful handover preserves cavity identity, onset time, material identity, restart context, available process signals and the supplier guidance consulted. It distinguishes a measured observation from an interpretation such as “hot-runner degradation.” If the evidence cannot separate local residence from a material or restart effect, record that uncertainty and seek the authorised supplier or tooling support before making a hardware change.

Keep a concise comparison table for each run: cavity and mark location, material and colour context, interruption/restart sequence, available zone or process records, and the last known-good observation. Do not assume all cavities share an identical local thermal history simply because they share controller targets. Equally, a cavity pattern alone is not proof of a particular drop fault. The purpose of the map is to show what follows the cavity, what follows time, and what follows material. That makes a supplier conversation or tooling review more specific without turning a symptom into an unsupported hardware diagnosis.

chapters.applicability: Framework for documenting a stable starting condition; not a recipe for selecting material-specific setpoints.

sections.title: Define the baseline as an evidence package
sections.text: A baseline is a defined record of a process that repeatedly makes parts meeting the stated checks under stated conditions. It includes exact material and lot, machine and mould identity, commands, measured signals, cycle conditions, cavity identity, inspection method and known limits. A single good part or a copied recipe is not a baseline. Establish what “normal” means by observing enough comparable cycles and parts to see natural variation. Mark what has not been verified so later comparisons do not treat assumptions as facts.

sections.title: Establish repeatability before comparing small effects
sections.text: Warm-up, material transition, recovery behaviour, mould temperature and recent interruptions can all move while the machine displays nominally stable commands. Use an appropriate sequence of repeated observations to determine whether the process is sufficiently steady for the comparison being made.

sections.title: Separate commanded settings from observed behaviour
sections.text: A set velocity, pressure, time or temperature is an instruction to the system, not proof that the intended physical state occurred. Where important, pair commands with observable responses such as actual positions, times, pressures, temperatures or part measurements. This prevents a baseline from becoming a list of unverified intentions.

sections.title: Record known boundaries and exclusions
sections.text: Document the supplier, machine, mould, hot-runner and site requirements that limit the experiment. If an important condition is unknown or not measured, state that explicitly. A baseline becomes more trustworthy when its uncertainties are visible rather than silently assumed away.

sections.title: What evidence should invalidate the baseline?
sections.text: Re-establish the baseline after material changes, significant maintenance, tooling changes, sensor or calibration changes, major thermal drift or other events that alter the population being compared. Historical settings should not be treated as current evidence when the physical system has materially changed.

chapters.applicability: Experimental method; exact procedure and stopping criteria depend on machine, mould and material.

sections.title: Purpose
sections.text: A fill study records progressive cavity filling under a defined, approved comparison. It helps reveal where the flow front travels and whether cavities or regions fill at different rates. It is descriptive evidence: it does not by itself prove a root cause, establish a production recipe or show that a short-filled sample represents normal production.

sections.title: Control the comparison
sections.text: State the question, the machine and mould identities, exact material and lot, sample sequence, cavity labels and measurement method. Keep relevant conditions constant and change only the authorized study factor. Capture the machine traces and part photographs alongside each sample. Work under site procedures and an approved study plan; never use this text to choose a setting or bypass a safeguard.

sections.title: Interpret cautiously
sections.text: Look for a progression that fits the hypothesized flow path, then compare it with pressure or motion signals where available. Check whether the pattern repeats and whether one cavity differs. A single incomplete sample may reflect handling, material delivery or a transient event. If the evidence does not distinguish those possibilities, revise the study rather than presenting an uncertain interpretation as fact.

chapters.applicability: Diagnostic study framework; measured pressures and safe limits are machine- and mould-specific.

sections.title: Every restriction changes the pressure demand
sections.text: As melt moves through a channel, pressure is needed to overcome viscous resistance and local losses. Smaller or longer paths, turns, junctions and gates can increase demand, but the result also depends on grade, temperature and flow rate. A larger pressure reading therefore does not point to one unique restriction. Compare equivalent states and use a model or measurement with clearly stated assumptions.

sections.title: Segment the path
sections.text: Draw the route from the machine nozzle to the part and identify where pressure is measured: machine-side, nozzle, runner or cavity. Separate the path into segments such as nozzle, sprue, runner, junction, gate and cavity. Ask which measured signal can observe each segment and what remains inferred. A known geometry change or cavity pattern can guide the next measurement, but do not assume pressure losses can be apportioned exactly without appropriate data.

sections.title: Do not equate machine pressure with cavity pressure
sections.text: Machine hydraulic pressure, screw pressure, nozzle pressure and cavity pressure are different quantities or signals, with different conversion and measurement locations. A controller may display a calculated value. Confirm units, sensor type, calibration and timing before comparison. Use cavity pressure only for the location where the sensor is installed. Treat discrepancies as evidence about the measurement chain and path, not as a reason to copy another machine’s limit.

chapters.applicability: Experimental determination for a specific material, gate and mould. No universal hold time applies.

sections.title: Why gate state matters
sections.text: The gate connects the runner to the cavity. While it transmits useful flow, hold pressure can continue to feed material as the part contracts. As the gate cools or otherwise closes to flow, further hold time may no longer change the part’s mass or a chosen response. Gate sealing depends on grade, gate geometry, thermal conditions and the measurement method, so no universal time applies.

sections.title: Use part response
sections.text: A controlled gate-seal study commonly compares part mass across planned hold-time conditions, with consistent cavity, conditioning, weighing and material history. Repeat measurements to establish whether a difference is larger than measurement variation. Part mass is a useful proxy for continued feeding but does not directly show gate temperature or internal quality. Use other product measurements when mass alone cannot answer the product question.

sections.title: Plateau is evidence, not a universal constant
sections.text: A plateau means the chosen response no longer changed detectably over the tested range for that mould, material, machine and conditions. It does not prove every cavity seals identically or that all critical dimensions have stabilized. Check cavity identity, sample size, balance, process stability and measurement resolution. Record the tested range and uncertainty, and keep the conclusion limited to that study.

chapters.applicability: Statistical/experimental concept. Acceptable limits must be tied to product requirements and equipment/material constraints.

sections.title: A setting is not a process window
sections.text: A process window is a tested region in which a defined output remains acceptable despite expected variation. It is more than one successful setting. Start by naming the part characteristics, measurements, cavities, material lot and conditions that define success; then challenge meaningful boundaries under a controlled, approved study. The edges matter because they show sensitivity and robustness. A window applies only to the tested system and ranges, so document what changed, what remained fixed, uncertainty and conditions that would require revalidation.

sections.title: Define outputs first
sections.text: Use measurable part requirements and process signals to determine what acceptable means. Cosmetic acceptance alone may miss dimensional or functional changes.

sections.title: Challenge the edges deliberately
sections.text: Controlled experiments can explore sensitivity to important variables, but only inside safe machine, mould and material limits. Document the tested region instead of claiming untested robustness.

sections.title: Worked example (hypothetical): build a process window from a sequence of questions
sections.text:
A team receives a new mould and wants to know whether the process is robust. “Find the best settings” is too broad to guide a useful study. Begin with the product requirements and the responses that can show whether they are met. The acceptance limits come from the approved product and quality requirements, not from the experimenter's preferred values.

The first question might be whether the cavity fills in a repeatable way before later packing effects dominate. A controlled fill study can describe how the flow front progresses while keeping the other relevant conditions as steady as practical. The observations can include fill pattern, part response and suitable machine signals, while recognising that an upstream signal does not prove local cavity pressure.

A second question might be where pressure demand increases along the flow path. Compare controlled states or appropriately located measurements, and keep machine-side pressure distinct from cavity pressure. A later question might be whether extending post-fill influence changes a defined part response. A hold-duration comparison can provide evidence about a plateau for that material, gate and thermal state; the result is not a universal hold time.

Only after those mechanisms are understood should the team ask how much normal variation the process can tolerate. Define the important input changes, the outputs that matter, the limits that govern the study and the evidence that would count as a failed edge. Explore within authorised material, machine, mould and site constraints. Preserve material condition, thermal state, cavity identity and measurement method so that the comparison remains interpretable.

Suppose the tested region produces acceptable measured outputs at several conditions, while one edge begins to approach a product limit. The result is a bounded map of what was actually studied, not proof that every untested combination will work. Confirm the conclusion with suitable repeated evidence and document its scope. If the material, mould, machine or measurement method changes materially, the old map may no longer describe the new system.

The tested region should be reported in the language of the study. State which input conditions were varied, which were held stable, which cavities and samples were included, how the outputs were measured, and which edges were actually challenged. If the study stopped before an edge because of a machine, mould, supplier or site limit, say so. A safe limit is not an invitation to test beyond it. The conclusion should describe the observed region and its evidence, not label the process “robust” outside the explored conditions. A later confirmation can check whether the response persists, but it does not erase the original scope.

Variation between cavities or runs should stay visible while the study is interpreted. Do not pool results until the team has checked that the samples represent the same intended population and comparable thermal and measurement conditions. A single sample can show that one condition produced one result; it cannot show how the process responds to normal variation. Repeat observations and confirmation should be chosen for the study and product risk, with the method documented. There is no universal repetition count in this example.

chapters.applicability: General documentation framework; regulated products and site quality systems may require additional records.

sections.title: Record the reasoning, not only the final setting
sections.text: Useful process records let another person reconstruct what was asked, what the machine did and what the parts showed. Record the meaning and units of signals, sensor location, machine and mould identity, material and lot, cavity labels, measurement method, date, operator context and study purpose. Include unsuccessful or inconclusive trials because they constrain explanations. Keep observations separate from interpretations, and mark uncertainty explicitly. A set of final numbers without context is difficult to reproduce and can be unsafe to transfer to another machine or part.

sections.title: Make records comparable over time
sections.text: Use stable names, units, cavity identifiers, measurement methods and version references so records from different shifts or maintenance states can be compared. Where controlled documents or quality systems apply, preserve revision and approval boundaries. A complete checkbox without traceable evidence is weaker than a concise record that shows what was observed and why the conclusion was reached.

sections.title: Document meaning, not only controller labels
sections.text: Two machines can use different names, scaling or reference points for apparently similar parameters. A useful record states what the value represents, where it is measured or commanded, its units and any conversion or interpretation used. This makes later comparison possible without assuming controller labels are equivalent.

sections.title: Record negative and inconclusive results
sections.text: A test that does not change the response can still eliminate a hypothesis. Keep negative and inconclusive evidence instead of documenting only successful adjustments. This reduces repeated experiments and helps future troubleshooting start from what is already known.

sections.title: Make uncertainty visible
sections.text: Where a measurement is approximate, a sensor is uncalibrated for the required inference, or a cause remains unresolved, state that limitation directly. A defensible process record separates measured fact, interpretation and assumption instead of presenting all three as equivalent.

sections.title: Worked example (hypothetical): hand over a baseline another shift can interpret
sections.text:
Imagine one shift reports that a dimensional change began after a maintenance event. The record contains a controller screenshot and the final setting values, but it does not identify the material lot, the cavity, the time after moulding when dimensions were checked, or whether the displayed values were commands or measured responses. A second shift cannot tell whether it is comparing the same physical state.

A useful handover would separate four things. First, identify context: material and lot, preparation history, machine, mould, cavity and relevant maintenance or interruption. Second, record the commanded conditions with units and controller meaning. Third, record the observed response: actual machine signals where available, sample identity, measurement method and part results. Fourth, state the interpretation and its uncertainty. A statement such as “the pressure increased” needs a signal location and measurement meaning before it can be compared across machines.

The record should also preserve the question being investigated, the change made, the expected observation and what actually happened. If the expected change did not occur, keep that result. It may weaken a hypothesis even when it does not solve the production problem. If a sensor was unavailable or the sample was not measured at the required reference condition, state that limitation instead of filling the gap with an assumption.

This example does not create a universal checklist. A regulated or customer-controlled process may require additional records and approvals. The useful test is whether another competent person can reconstruct the comparison, see which facts were measured, distinguish them from interpretation, and decide whether the old baseline still applies after the maintenance event.

A compact handover can use labelled fields rather than a long narrative: question; last known-good state; material and preparation; machine and mould; commanded values and units; observed signals and their locations; cavity/sample identifiers; measurement conditions; change and prediction; result; uncertainty; next authorised action. Empty fields should be marked “not measured” or “unknown,” not silently treated as normal. A reader should be able to distinguish “the display showed the requested value” from “the physical response was verified.” That distinction is especially useful when another shift repeats the study or when an old record is compared after maintenance.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: General troubleshooting method; safety and product-disposition decisions remain under site procedures.

sections.title: Use chronology to reduce the search space
sections.text: Start with the last known good part or cycle, then mark when the defect or signal changed. Record shifts, interruptions, material lot changes, tool interventions and measurement changes in order. Chronology helps divide the problem into earlier and later conditions, but correlation with a date or shift does not prove cause. Keep the timeline factual and attach evidence to each event.

sections.title: Prefer tests that can falsify a favourite explanation
sections.text: For each plausible mechanism, write down what you expect to observe if it is true and what result would weaken it. A useful test separates competing explanations; a change that merely makes the part look better can leave the cause unknown. Choose the least risky measurement that can answer the question, and have the authorized process owner approve any trial.

sections.title: Escalate when the evidence boundary is reached
sections.text: Pause the investigation if the next step requires entering a guarded area, changing tooling, exceeding a documented limit, handling a hazardous material or accepting uncertain product risk. Route the evidence to the qualified person responsible for machine safety, tooling, material or product approval. Escalation is a decision point, not a failure of diagnosis.

sections.title: Characterise the defect before naming a cause
sections.text: Describe the symptom by location, direction, size, frequency, cavity, time of appearance and measurement method. Photograph or map it against a part drawing and keep representative samples. Words such as “burn,” “splay” or “short” describe appearances; they do not prove mechanism. A precise description gives different investigators the same starting point.

sections.title: Use boundaries to shrink the search space
sections.text: Compare affected and unaffected populations: cavity, shift, material lot, start-up versus steady state, before versus after a pause, or one geometry region versus another. Keep the comparison fair by checking that the samples were produced and measured under comparable conditions. A boundary is useful only when the group labels are reliable.

sections.title: Write predicted observations for competing mechanisms
sections.text: An upstream delivery problem might affect several cavities together; a local vent or gate issue might follow one region. Those are possible predictions, not universal rules. Write the expected pattern for each hypothesis using the actual mould layout and machine signals. Also state what else could create the same pattern. This makes the test plan explicit and guards against post-hoc storytelling.

sections.title: Choose tests that discriminate, not merely improve
sections.text: Prefer a measurement whose possible outcomes point in different directions. Examples include cavity-resolved part mass, fill progression, pressure traces at known locations, or dimensional checks at a defined conditioning time. Each method has limitations; record resolution and uncertainty. If a test cannot distinguish the leading explanations, do not overstate its result.

sections.title: Confirm recovery and record uncertainty
sections.text: After a controlled correction, verify that the part meets the required checks over the population and time window relevant to the decision. Confirm the original symptom has not moved or been replaced by another defect. Record what changed, what stayed constant, the evidence supporting the conclusion and remaining uncertainty. A successful run is evidence of recovery under those conditions, not proof that no other mechanism exists.

sections.title: Worked example (hypothetical): a short shot appears after an interruption
sections.text: In a hypothetical case, short shots begin after a production pause. The timeline suggests several candidates: material residence, a restart sequence, a transient machine condition or a sensor issue. The investigator first compares affected cavities and restart cycles, then checks approved traces and the exact material instructions. A test is selected to distinguish a common upstream shift from a local flow restriction. No one changes settings until the machine owner approves the study. The example demonstrates reasoning order, not a restart recipe.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Diagnostic hypotheses for incomplete filling; actual corrective action depends on the identified restriction and equipment limits.

sections.title: What it tells you
sections.text: A short shot is an incompletely filled part, which tells you where the flow stopped but not why it stopped. Possible causes include insufficient delivered material, restricted flow, trapped gas, a machine limit, unstable material condition or a process transition occurring at the wrong point. Map the missing region, compare cavities and cycles, and inspect the fill trace and material path. Distinguish repeatable shortage from intermittent loss before changing the process. Do not hide a restriction by indiscriminately raising settings.

sections.title: Mechanisms to distinguish
sections.text: Possible mechanisms include insufficient delivered material, premature transfer, inadequate flow capability, excessive restriction, loss of venting effectiveness, material/melt condition or machine delivery problems.

sections.title: Separate command limits from delivered process
sections.text: Check whether the machine actually reached the commanded velocity, position and pressure behaviour and whether transfer or protection limits intervened. A short shot can occur even with apparently generous setpoints if the effective shot, flow path, material state or machine delivery differs from the assumption. Measured response is therefore more informative than the setting alone.

sections.title: Separate repeatable shortage from intermittent loss
sections.text: A consistently unfilled region can indicate a stable restriction, thermal condition, shot-delivery limit or venting problem. An intermittent short shot can point toward inconsistent check-valve behaviour, material feed, transfer repeatability, air, machine delivery or changing mould conditions. Time-order the events rather than pooling good and bad cycles; intermittency itself is evidence about the mechanism.

sections.title: Separate delivered-material problems from flow-path problems
sections.text: Incomplete filling can result because too little material is delivered, because transfer occurs before the intended fill state, or because the available flow capability cannot overcome the actual restriction and thermal condition. Compare shot delivery, screw/cushion behaviour, transfer position, fill pattern and pressure demand before deciding which category is more plausible.

sections.title: Use cavity and time patterns
sections.text: In a multi-cavity tool, one persistently short cavity suggests a local balance, restriction, venting or thermal issue more strongly than a whole-mould event. If every cavity becomes short together after a material, machine or thermal change, a common upstream mechanism deserves more attention. Pattern is evidence, not proof, but it helps prioritise safe tests.

sections.title: Read pressure demand together with fill progression
sections.text: Pressure by itself does not identify the restriction. A rising upstream pressure demand with limited additional fill can support the presence of an increasingly restrictive flow path, but the same signal can be influenced by material condition, temperature, rate and machine behaviour. Combine pressure response with controlled short-shot progression and physical inspection.

sections.title: Do not hide a restriction with indiscriminate settings
sections.text: Increasing pressure, speed or temperature can sometimes extend fill, but it can also mask a blocked gate, poor venting, material-preparation problem or machine-delivery fault and may create new defects. Establish the mechanism first and keep all tests inside machine, mould, material and site limits.

sections.title: Evidence that should move the investigation elsewhere
sections.text: Reconsider the leading hypothesis when the symptom does not follow its predicted boundary, when delivery measurements remain stable despite a delivery theory, when cleaning or thermal stabilisation changes only one cavity, or when the pressure/fill relationship does not behave as expected. The purpose of the investigation is to eliminate explanations as well as support them.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Diagnostic hypotheses only. Never exceed machine or mould limits to suppress or create flash.

sections.title: What flash means
sections.text: Flash is excess material at a mould boundary or opening. Its location and timing help distinguish a local parting-line or support issue from pressure, viscosity, alignment or damage-related mechanisms. Map the flash on the actual part and mould location, then compare it with cavity-pressure or machine evidence where available. A change that reduces flash can still create an underfilled part, damage the tool or mask a mechanical problem. Use approved containment and have tooling and process specialists review the evidence before changing force or steel.

sections.title: Competing causes
sections.text: Tool damage or mismatch, inadequate clamping condition, excessive cavity pressure, over-packing, low melt viscosity and contamination at shutoff surfaces can produce similar symptoms.

sections.title: Treat process compensation as evidence, not proof
sections.text: If a pressure or temperature change reduces flash, that shows the defect responds to the process state but does not prove the mould is healthy or identify the root cause. Verify whether the corrected condition remains inside the qualified process window and whether tooling inspection is warranted before institutionalising compensation.

sections.title: Parting-line support and local pressure matter
sections.text: A mould can experience local opening or material escape even when the nominal machine clamp setting appears adequate. Local geometry, support, wear, contamination and pressure distribution influence what happens at a specific region. Because pressure falls through the flow path and varies with time, a machine pressure display cannot by itself establish the local force acting where flash appears.

sections.title: Verify the fix does not create a new defect
sections.text: A change that removes flash can also alter fill balance, packing, dimensions, residual stress or mould protection margin. Re-check the product characteristics and process signals that matter after any corrective trial. A defensible fix should restore the intended boundary without merely moving the process to another edge of its operating window.

sections.title: Map the flash before changing clamp or packing
sections.text: Record whether flash occurs at the parting line, around an insert, at a shutoff, near a slide or in one local region. Note whether it is present from start-up, appears after thermal stabilisation, or begins after a process or tooling event. Location and onset help distinguish a mechanical gap from a pressure-history problem.

sections.title: Clamp force is not an unlimited corrective lever
sections.text: The useful question is whether the mould is being adequately and safely closed under the real projected-area and pressure conditions, not whether the machine can simply be commanded to a larger number. Machine, mould and site limits remain controlling, and local flash can persist even when overall clamp capacity is adequate.

sections.title: Viscosity and contamination can change the symptom
sections.text: A lower-resistance melt can enter gaps that a more viscous condition did not, while contamination on a shutoff can create or enlarge the effective gap. These mechanisms can produce similar visual results but require different evidence and different corrective action.

sections.title: When the flash diagnosis should change
sections.text: Revisit the conclusion if the flash stays fixed to a damaged location despite process changes, disappears after shutoff cleaning, moves with a change in cavity pressure history, or appears only after thermal growth. A credible diagnosis must explain both where the flash occurs and why its timing changes.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Mechanism guidance for thermoplastic parts; acceptance and correction depend on geometry, material and product requirements.

sections.title: Sink and internal voids are related but not identical
sections.text: A sink mark is a visible surface depression; a void is an internal gap. Both can be associated with contraction in a thick region, but one does not prove the other. Geometry, local cooling, gate location and the ability to feed material during packing influence where the symptom develops. Compare part section, location, weight and time response; use suitable internal inspection when product risk warrants it. Learn to distinguish visible evidence from internal structure before deciding whether the problem is cosmetic, dimensional or structural.

sections.title: Use section location and time response
sections.text: Map the defect against thick sections, ribs, bosses, gate distance and cooling features. Then compare the response to controlled packing and cooling changes within safe limits. If additional post-fill pressure no longer affects the region, the feed path may no longer transmit useful pressure; that is a different conclusion from assuming more hold time is always beneficial.

sections.title: Gate location and feed path shape the packing opportunity
sections.text: Pressure can compensate for volumetric contraction only while an effective feed path remains available to the region. Distance from the gate, section thickness, gate freezing and local resistance all affect how much post-fill influence reaches a thick feature. This is why a sink or void investigation should consider geometry and the pressure path, not only the nominal hold setting.

sections.title: Separate feed effectiveness from local geometry
sections.text: If a thick region continues to contract after the gate or feed path no longer transmits useful pressure, extending hold time may not change the outcome. Conversely, if the region is still pressure-responsive, packing evidence may matter. Compare part mass, local dimensions, gate-response studies and defect location so that the diagnosis distinguishes inadequate pressure transmission from a geometry or cooling limitation.

sections.title: Use sectioning or suitable inspection when the product risk justifies it
sections.text: Surface appearance cannot always distinguish an internal void from acceptable internal structure. Where the product requirement makes hidden porosity important, use an appropriate inspection method and define the acceptance criterion. The Book can explain the mechanism, but product-specific disposition remains controlled by the applicable quality requirement.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Diagnostic framework. Moisture limits and drying conditions are grade-specific.

sections.title: Material evidence first
sections.text: Splay is a surface appearance that often looks like streaks or silvering, but it is a symptom rather than a diagnosis. Moisture, volatile material, shear, trapped gas, contamination and degradation can produce overlapping appearances. Start by recording the pattern and cavity distribution, then trace the exact grade and material handling history. Check supplier drying and storage limits rather than guessing or over-drying. A controlled comparison should predict what changes if the leading explanation is true and preserve evidence about material, machine and mould conditions.

sections.title: Avoid over-drying by guesswork
sections.text: Drying hotter or longer is not universally safer; excessive thermal exposure can also damage some materials. Follow grade-specific documentation.

sections.title: Splay is an appearance, not a root cause
sections.text: Silver or streaked surface patterns can be consistent with moisture, other volatiles, air entrainment, decompression effects, contamination or degradation. Use location, material history, lot pattern, dryer evidence, residence history and process timing to discriminate among mechanisms. Avoid converting a familiar visual pattern into an automatic drying diagnosis.

sections.title: Ask what should change if the hypothesis is true
sections.text: A moisture hypothesis predicts a relationship with verified material condition; a degradation hypothesis predicts a relationship with thermal history; an air-entrapment hypothesis may follow geometry or decompression conditions. Controlled evidence that separates these predictions is stronger than repeated parameter changes that all alter the appearance.

sections.title: Use material handling as a traceable variable
sections.text: If a volatile or moisture mechanism is suspected, record when the material was opened, dried, transferred, exposed and returned to the hopper, together with any verified moisture result where appropriate. A traceable material-handling history allows the symptom to be compared with real state changes instead of relying on memory or the assumption that dryer settings always represent material condition.

sections.title: Follow the symptom through material and machine boundaries
sections.text: Ask whether the streak follows a material container, dryer, machine, cavity, restart or process state. A symptom that moves with the material supports a different hypothesis from one that remains with one mould or appears only after decompression or residence changes. This boundary analysis helps prevent repeated drying changes when the dominant mechanism lies elsewhere.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Diagnostic hypotheses for dark/burned areas; purge and intervention procedures remain machine/site specific.

sections.title: Distinguish compressed gas from thermal degradation
sections.text: A dark or scorched end-of-fill mark may result from compressed trapped gas, but thermal degradation, contamination and other material histories can create similar defects. The part location is a clue: relate it to the last area filled, vent paths, cavity pattern and recent process interruptions. Ask whether the symptom follows one cavity or all cavities and whether it appears after a hot wait. Keep vent hypotheses separate from material hypotheses, and do not alter tooling or purge procedures without qualified approval.

sections.title: Vent work is tooling work
sections.text: When evidence points toward restricted venting, inspection or modification must follow approved tooling and safety procedures. Generic teaching can explain why gas escape matters and how a pattern may support the hypothesis; it cannot prescribe unreviewed vent dimensions or authorise cutting steel.

sections.title: End-of-fill location is a clue, not proof
sections.text: A recurring mark at the last region to fill can support a trapped-gas hypothesis, especially when vent condition or fill sequence changes the outcome. But degraded material can also collect in difficult regions. Confirm the pattern across cavities, cycles and interventions before converting location into a root-cause claim.

sections.title: Use chronology to distinguish trapped gas from degraded material
sections.text: A repeatable mark at the same end-of-fill location from the first stable cycles supports a different investigation from dark material that appears after a pause and then diminishes. Record where the mark occurs, when it begins and whether it follows material residence or cavity geometry. The chronology should fit the proposed mechanism before corrective action is treated as confirmed.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: General flow-front mechanism; strength/appearance impact depends on material, geometry and product requirement.

sections.title: A weld line records a flow-front meeting event
sections.text: A weld line forms where separated flow fronts meet, for example after flowing around a hole or joining from multiple gates. Its visible appearance alone does not reveal bond strength. Front temperature, pressure, contamination, geometry, venting, material formulation and orientation can all affect the interface. Locate the line on the part drawing, identify the flow paths that meet there and define the actual performance requirement. Cosmetic improvement is not proof of structural adequacy; testing must match the product risk and specification.

sections.title: When to reconsider the weld-line mechanism
sections.text: Revise the working explanation when the line location does not follow expected flow-front changes, when strength does not track appearance, or when cavity and vent patterns contradict the assumed mechanism. Escalate to design, tooling, material or simulation evidence where process observations cannot discriminate the cause.

sections.title: Flow-front temperature is only part of the story
sections.text: The ability of two fronts to form a useful interface depends on local thermal and pressure history, material condition, contamination, venting and the way orientation develops as the fronts meet. Raising a nominal melt or mould setting can alter some of these factors, but it is not a universal weld-line cure. The actual material and product requirement determine whether appearance, strength, sealing or another response is the critical outcome.

sections.title: Use testing that matches the real product risk
sections.text: A weld line that looks improved may still have inadequate mechanical performance, and a visible line may be acceptable where the part is not structurally limited. Select measurements that represent the actual requirement, such as relevant dimensional, leak, impact, tensile or functional testing where applicable. Avoid using appearance alone as a universal proxy for interface quality.

sections.title: Gas and venting belong in the diagnosis
sections.text: When fronts converge, displaced gas must still escape. A weak or marked interface near the end of a flow region can therefore involve both front temperature and gas evacuation. Inspect vent condition and the local fill sequence before assuming that a single temperature increase is the correct response.

sections.title: Use discriminating evidence
sections.text: Compare line location, repeatability, filling pattern, vent condition, material state and controlled changes that alter front arrival conditions. A useful test should predict whether the interface moves, becomes more or less pronounced, or remains unchanged. If the observed behaviour contradicts the proposed mechanism, revise the diagnosis instead of adding more settings changes.

sections.title: Process windows matter more than one cosmetic optimum
sections.text: A change that improves weld-line appearance at one operating point may reduce robustness elsewhere. Evaluate the response over a defensible process range and against the real product requirement. The preferred condition is one that maintains acceptable interface performance while preserving other quality characteristics, not simply the setting that makes one sample look best.

sections.title: Verify the interface against the real product requirement
sections.text: The engineering question is not simply whether a weld line can be seen. Define whether the requirement is cosmetic, dimensional, pressure-tight, fatigue-related or structural, then use an appropriate measurement or test. A process change that makes the line visually weaker or stronger may not produce the same change in the property that matters to the product.

sections.title: Worked example (hypothetical): assess a line downstream of a hole
sections.text:
Consider a part with a hole that divides the advancing melt into two fronts. The fronts later meet downstream, where a visible line appears. The location is consistent with a flow-front meeting, but appearance alone does not establish whether the interface meets the product requirement or which process or design factor matters most.

Begin with the geometry-fixed evidence. Mark the hole, gates, flow directions, meeting region and any nearby vent path on a part drawing. Check whether the line repeats in the same place across cavities and runs. Then describe its appearance separately from its performance consequence. A cosmetic requirement, a pressure-tight requirement and a structural requirement call for different evidence and acceptance criteria.

Next list hypotheses that make different predictions. A change in front-arrival conditions may alter the line's position or appearance. A gas-evacuation issue may fit the meeting region and vent condition. Material or thermal history may affect how the interface develops. None should be accepted merely because a setting change improves one sample. Compare the observed line with fill sequence, cavity pattern, material state and available pressure or temperature evidence, using measurements whose location and meaning are understood.

Choose a test that answers a defined question and stays inside authorised limits. If the product risk is mechanical or sealing, select a product-relevant test through the appropriate engineering and quality authority; visual inspection cannot substitute for that decision. Preserve the tested material, mould, cavity, process window and sample condition so the conclusion stays bounded to the evidence.

If the line moves but the required performance does not change, appearance and function may be responding differently. If appearance improves while another product characteristic moves toward its limit, the change is not a complete solution. The handover should state what was observed, what was measured, which explanation gained or lost support, and what remains unresolved. This worked example does not recommend a gate, vent, temperature or pressure change.

For a beginner, it helps to keep three records side by side: a marked-up drawing of where the fronts meet, a description of the line in repeat parts, and the product test or inspection that represents the actual risk. A change that moves the line may be useful evidence about flow, while a change that alters measured performance addresses a different question. If these records disagree, preserve the disagreement. It may show that the visible feature and the relevant product response are not controlled by the same factor. The next study should target that difference rather than repeat a cosmetic adjustment.
