chapters.applicability: General mechanism and measurement framework. Prediction requires actual material, geometry, mould and process data.

sections.title: Warpage is differential deformation
sections.text: Warpage is a shape change caused by unequal shrinkage, stiffness or restraint across a part. Cooling gradients, packing differences, molecular or fibre orientation, geometry and post-ejection conditioning can all contribute, often together. First describe the direction and magnitude of the shape change, when it is measured, and how the part is supported. Compare cavities and locations before selecting a mechanism. A process adjustment can move the distortion rather than remove it, so connect every trial to a measured shape profile and intended product requirement.

sections.title: Build a mechanism map before changing the process
sections.text: Separate plausible contributors into material, flow/orientation, packing, mould thermal balance, cooling geometry, wall-thickness distribution, ejection restraint and post-mould conditioning. More than one mechanism can act at the same time, and correcting one may expose another.

sections.title: Measure shape, direction and time
sections.text: Define datum strategy, measurement method, conditioning state, time after moulding and the direction/magnitude of deformation. A part measured hot, immediately after ejection or after moisture conditioning is not automatically comparable with a part measured under a different reference condition.

sections.title: Use cavity and time patterns to discriminate causes
sections.text: A repeatable bias in one cavity suggests a different investigation from a drift shared by every cavity as the mould warms. Directional deformation aligned with flow can support an orientation hypothesis, while local distortion around thick sections can support a thermal or shrinkage-gradient hypothesis. These patterns guide testing but do not prove cause by themselves.

sections.title: Change one mechanism-relevant variable at a time where practical
sections.text: Use controlled comparisons that are capable of producing different predictions for competing hypotheses. Examples include comparing cavity-specific dimensional vectors, stable mould-temperature conditions, packing response, cooling balance or conditioning time while remaining inside approved equipment, material and product limits.

sections.title: Evidence that weakens the current warpage hypothesis
sections.text: Revise the diagnosis when measured deformation does not follow the predicted direction, cavity pattern, thermal trend or process response. If several mechanisms remain consistent with the observations, preserve the uncertainty and escalate to additional measurement, tooling inspection, material evidence or simulation instead of forcing a single root cause.

sections.title: Restraint can hide or release distortion
sections.text: Fixtures, packaging, assembly features and even the mould itself can restrain a part while stresses and shrinkage differences develop. When that restraint is removed, measured shape can change. Record whether the part was measured free, fixtured or assembled, and compare equivalent conditions before attributing a shape difference solely to the moulding cycle.

sections.title: Design and process effects can be inseparable
sections.text: Wall-thickness transitions, ribs, bosses, gating and reinforcement orientation create local conditions that process settings can influence but not always eliminate. When a stable process repeatedly produces the same distortion pattern, the evidence may point toward a geometry or tooling contribution rather than inadequate optimisation. Escalation to design or tooling review is a valid engineering outcome.

sections.title: Worked example (hypothetical): a reinforced panel bows after release
sections.text:
A reinforced panel looks flat while restrained in a fixture but bows after it is released. Record both observations and the exact measurement condition. A restrained shape and a free shape answer different questions; neither alone identifies why the part changed.

Keep cavity identity, material lot, measurement direction and time after moulding with each result. Compare whether the bow follows flow direction, a thick feature, one cavity or all cavities. A directional pattern can motivate an orientation question; a local pattern near a thickness change can motivate a cooling or geometry question. A shared change across cavities may point toward a common thermal or material condition. These are ways to organise tests, not proof of cause.

The next comparison should distinguish the leading explanations. Use an equivalent fixture and datum strategy, measure under the product's defined reference conditions, and preserve the same part orientation. If the result changes with conditioning time, record that profile instead of treating one convenient measurement as final. If the distortion remains cavity-specific under controlled measurement, keep tooling and local process evidence in the investigation.

Do not treat a single process adjustment as confirmation merely because one sample looks flatter. The example asks what evidence would separate restraint, orientation, cooling and cavity effects; the approved product requirement determines acceptance.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Diagnostic hypotheses. Purging, disassembly and maintenance must use approved machine/material procedures.

sections.title: What the defect suggests
sections.text: Black specks are visible contamination or discoloration, not a single root cause. They may originate in degraded material, retained residue, external contamination, a hot runner, the screw or barrel, or handling. Map whether specks occur in every cavity, at one location, only after a pause or throughout the run. Preserve representative samples and timeline evidence before repeated purging or cleaning removes clues. Never use a diagnostic action that bypasses a site safety procedure or the material supplier’s system-specific instructions.

sections.title: Do not create a safety problem while diagnosing
sections.text: Hot purging, nozzle work and barrel intervention involve machine-specific hazards. Follow authorised procedures instead of improvised cleaning methods.

sections.title: Cleaning success does not automatically prove origin
sections.text: A purge or cleaning action that reduces specks shows the defect is responsive to that intervention but may not identify the original source. Confirm whether recurrence follows residence, shutdown, hot-runner state, material handling or another boundary. Persistent recurrence deserves equipment or tooling inspection rather than an endless purge cycle.

sections.title: Create a source map before repeated purging
sections.text: List every plausible point where foreign or degraded material could enter the melt path: material handling, feed throat, screw/barrel, nozzle, manifold, drops and cavity-specific regions. Then use the cavity and time pattern to remove unlikely locations. This makes cleaning or inspection targeted and reduces the risk of repeatedly purging without learning where the contamination originates.

sections.title: Worked example (hypothetical): compare an all-cavity event with a one-cavity event
sections.text:
A quality report describes dark specks, but the complaint combines parts from every cavity and several hours of production. Separate the observations before choosing a source. Two patterns can look similar on a finished part while pointing to different places in the material and moulding path.

In the first hypothetical pattern, specks begin after a material change and appear across several cavities. That does not prove the material is the source, but it makes the shared material path, changeover history and restart sequence relevant boundaries. Preserve the lot and handling record and compare the event with the last known-good state. In the second pattern, one cavity shows recurring specks while the others remain clear. That makes a local path or cavity-linked source worth investigating, without excluding a shared upstream cause that affects only part of the flow.

For both patterns, record when the defect starts, whether it persists or fades, the cavity identity, the material transition and any approved maintenance or inspection history. Then map plausible sources along the feed and melt path. The map should include material handling and machine or hot-runner locations where they apply, but it should not become an instruction to disassemble or purge equipment.

A cleaning action that reduces the specks would show that the symptom responded; it would not by itself prove where the contamination began. Follow approved machine and material procedures, preserve samples or records as required by the site, and escalate recurring events for authorised inspection. The useful outcome is a narrower, evidence-based source map, not a confident guess from colour alone.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Sensor-based process analysis. Sensor selection, installation, calibration and limits are manufacturer- and mould-specific.

sections.title: Sensor location defines what the trace means
sections.text: A cavity-pressure trace measures pressure at the sensor’s particular location and through its specific signal chain. Its value depends on sensor position, calibration, response, cavity and timing reference; it is not a universal picture of pressure everywhere in the mould. Establish a representative trace and check sensor health before setting limits. Compare meaningful features—such as onset, peak, transfer relation or decay—with cavity identity and part response. A changed trace is a prompt to investigate the process, not an automatic instruction to alter the machine.

sections.title: Establish a reference trace before using limits
sections.text: A pressure limit is most meaningful when derived from a known, stable process state and a defined sensor location. Record the material, thermal and process conditions associated with that state and understand normal cycle-to-cycle variation. Arbitrary limits based on one apparently good cycle can create nuisance alarms or miss meaningful drift.

sections.title: Compare features that have physical meaning
sections.text: Useful trace features can include arrival timing, pressure at a defined event, peak behaviour or decay characteristics where these are technically justified. Feature choice should correspond to a mechanism or product response, not simply to what the software can calculate. A mathematically convenient feature with no stable physical interpretation can create false confidence.

sections.title: Sensor health belongs in the diagnosis
sections.text: Mounting condition, preload, contamination, cable faults, drift or replacement can change the measured signal. When a pressure pattern changes unexpectedly, verify the measurement chain before concluding the process changed. Sensor maintenance and calibration requirements come from the applicable sensor and equipment documentation.

sections.title: Correlate to part response within a defined study window
sections.text: If a trace feature repeatedly corresponds with a measured part characteristic, that relationship can support monitoring or investigation within the studied range. Preserve the material, mould, sensor, cavity and operating-window context. A relationship observed in one window should not be promoted automatically into a universal quality rule.

sections.title: Use cavity pressure to discriminate upstream from local behaviour
sections.text: Comparing machine-side signals with cavity-side response can help show whether a change is occurring upstream, in the mould flow path or locally near the sensor. The comparison is most useful when signal timing, units and acquisition behaviour are known and repeatable.

sections.title: When the pressure interpretation should be revised
sections.text: Revisit the interpretation if calibration or sensor condition changes, the quality relationship breaks in confirmation data, another cavity behaves differently, or the same part response occurs without the expected trace feature. Monitoring rules require maintained evidence, not permanent assumptions.

sections.title: Worked example (hypothetical): interpret a changed trace before changing an alarm
sections.text:
A monitoring screen flags a pressure-trace change, but the machine-side injection-pressure display looks similar to its reference. First confirm which cavity sensor produced the trace, where it is mounted and whether the sensor and acquisition chain are in their expected condition. A cavity sensor describes pressure at its own location; it does not report one uniform value for the whole mould.

Compare the trace with a reference from a defined, stable state. Look at the timing and features that have a physical meaning for that sensor and study. Preserve cavity identity, material and thermal conditions, transfer behaviour and the corresponding part measurement. If the pressure trace changes but the measured part response does not, that may weaken a proposed quality relationship. If both move together repeatedly inside the studied range, the relationship may be useful for that bounded monitoring purpose.

Do not move the alarm limit simply to stop a nuisance alert. Ask whether the signal changed, the sensor changed, the process state changed, or the baseline was not representative. The alarm can prompt an investigation; it does not establish root cause or product disposition by itself. Document the next action that the alarm is intended to trigger and the evidence needed before a quality decision.

chapters.applicability: General experimental-design principles; experiment ranges must stay within safe and qualified limits.

sections.title: Why designed experiments help
sections.text: Design of experiments (DOE) studies several planned factors together so their effects and interactions can be separated more efficiently than by informal trial and error. A sound study begins with a real engineering question, measurable outputs, bounded factor ranges and a plan to handle nuisance variation. The model only speaks for the materials, machine, mould, ranges and conditions tested. Statistical significance does not automatically mean a useful or safe production change. Confirm conclusions with new runs and the required part checks before updating a baseline.

sections.title: Start with a process question, not a software design
sections.text: State the decision the experiment must support, define measurable responses and identify the mechanisms that could plausibly affect them. Then select factors, levels, blocking variables and replicates that can discriminate among those explanations. An elegant statistical design is weak if its factors do not represent the process physics.

sections.title: Protect the experiment from nuisance variation
sections.text: Material lot or moisture state, mould thermal condition, machine warm-up, cavity identity, operator sequence, measurement timing and ambient conditions can obscure the effects being studied. Randomisation, blocking and consistent preconditioning help prevent time trends or hidden groups from being mistaken for factor effects.

sections.title: Interpret interactions explicitly
sections.text: When the effect of one factor changes depending on the level of another, a main-effect average can be misleading. Review interaction plots, residual behavior and engineering mechanism together rather than converting one coefficient or p-value into a universal rule.

sections.title: Separate statistical significance from useful engineering change
sections.text: A detectable effect may be too small to matter to the product, while an important effect can be missed when measurement noise or sample size is inadequate. Report effect size, uncertainty, response variation and product relevance alongside significance tests.

sections.title: When the experimental model should lose authority
sections.text: Reconsider the model when residuals show structure, repeat runs disagree, the effect disappears under confirmation trials, factor changes produce physically implausible responses, or the tested range does not represent production. Confirmation runs and mechanism-consistent predictions are required before promoting an experimental result into a process rule.

sections.title: Factor ranges define the scope of the conclusion
sections.text: A DOE estimates behaviour over the levels actually studied. Extrapolating beyond those levels can be unsafe or technically wrong, especially when polymer flow, thermal response or machine limits are nonlinear. State the tested range with the conclusion and require new evidence before applying the result to a materially different process window.

sections.title: Use confirmation runs before turning effects into process rules
sections.text: After selecting a preferred factor combination or model, repeat the condition independently and compare the observed response with the prediction. Confirmation helps reveal time drift, hidden interactions or overfitting to the original data. A model that cannot predict a fresh run should be treated as incomplete evidence rather than promoted into a permanent process rule.

chapters.applicability: General quality-engineering concepts. Capability indices are meaningful only under their statistical assumptions and customer/site definitions.

sections.title: Stability and measurement credibility come first
sections.text: Capability describes the relationship between a stable process distribution and a specified product requirement. It does not establish that the measurement is trustworthy, the sample is representative or the process will stay stable. Confirm the measurement system, specification, time period, cavity mix and material/condition traceability first. Then examine the distribution and report the assumptions behind any index. A good number can conceal a cavity or time effect, and a high capability value cannot make an unsuitable tolerance or measurement method appropriate.

sections.title: Distinguish specification, control and process behavior
sections.text: Specification limits define acceptable product requirements; control limits describe expected process behavior under a chosen statistical model. They are not interchangeable. A process can be statistically stable yet incapable, or capable over a short sample while not being stable enough for a defensible long-term claim.

sections.title: Examine the distribution instead of assuming it
sections.text: Histogram shape, subgroup behavior, time order, outliers, multiple cavities and bounded measurements can violate simple normal and independent assumptions. Where assumptions do not fit, use an appropriate method and state it instead of reporting Cp/Cpk mechanically.

sections.title: Separate cavity and time effects
sections.text: Pooling multiple cavities or long periods into one calculation can hide systematic cavity offsets, warm-up effects, tool maintenance changes or material-lot shifts. Review cavity-level and time-ordered data before deciding which population a capability statement actually represents.

sections.title: Report the evidence behind the number
sections.text: A useful capability report includes the characteristic, specification basis, sampling plan, measurement method, process state, subgrouping, data period, excluded data with justification, chosen calculation method and uncertainty or confidence information where appropriate.

sections.title: Conditions that invalidate or qualify the capability claim
sections.text: Withdraw or qualify a capability claim when the process becomes unstable, the measurement system changes, cavity populations separate, the distribution model is poor, specifications are revised, or new data materially shifts the estimated performance. Capability is a maintained evidence statement, not a permanent property of the mould.

sections.title: Short-term and long-term capability answer different questions
sections.text: A short, tightly controlled study can describe performance under one stable operating period, while longer production data includes more sources of variation such as lots, maintenance states, shifts and environmental changes. Do not present a short-term result as if it automatically represents long-term production. State the data horizon and what sources of variation were included.

sections.title: Capability cannot rescue an unsuitable specification or measurement
sections.text: A high capability index is not meaningful if the specification basis is wrong, the characteristic is measured inconsistently or the data population combines incompatible conditions. Before optimising the number, verify the requirement, measurement system, sampling and process population. The statistical summary comes after those engineering decisions, not before them.

sections.title: Capability belongs to a defined population
sections.text: Always state what population the index represents: which cavity or cavities, what time period, material condition, machine state and measurement method. Combining unlike populations can produce a mathematically valid number that answers the wrong engineering question. The population definition is therefore part of the capability claim, not an optional note.

chapters.applicability: General monitoring architecture. Available signals, sampling rates and alarm actions depend on machine/controller and site quality system.

sections.title: Monitor signals tied to mechanisms
sections.text: Process monitoring is useful when each signal has a defined meaning and a decision attached to it. Choose signals that plausibly track the failure mechanism, verify the measurement chain and establish a representative baseline across normal variation. Separate an isolated event from a persistent shift, and retain cavity, time and material context. A threshold copied from another machine or product may create false alarms or miss meaningful change. Monitoring flags evidence for review; it does not diagnose root cause or authorize automatic machine control.

sections.title: Define the measurement chain
sections.text: Document where each signal originates, its units, sampling behavior, filtering, calibration status and any controller transformations. Machine injection pressure, hydraulic pressure, cavity pressure, screw position and derived metrics may describe different physical locations or calculations and should not be treated as interchangeable.

sections.title: Establish a representative baseline
sections.text: Build monitoring limits from a stable, qualified operating state rather than from arbitrary historical minimum and maximum values. Include normal sources of variation such as cavities, material lots and operating phases only when they belong to the population the monitoring rule is intended to represent.

sections.title: Detect drift separately from isolated events
sections.text: Single-cycle excursions, gradual thermal drift, step changes after maintenance and recurring cavity-specific patterns call for different investigations. Time plots, run rules and cavity stratification can reveal behavior that a single pass/fail limit hides.

sections.title: When the monitoring rule needs revision
sections.text: Revisit monitoring logic when alarms do not correspond to meaningful process or product changes, significant defects occur without signal movement, sensor behavior changes, or a new process state shifts the normal population. Monitoring models require maintenance just as the physical process does.

sections.title: Design monitoring around decisions
sections.text: Before collecting more signals, define the decision each signal is intended to support: detecting drift, protecting a process window, identifying a cavity deviation, prompting additional measurement or documenting production state. Monitoring that has no defined action can generate data without improving control. Conversely, an alarm should not trigger an automatic product conclusion unless that relationship has been separately validated.

sections.title: Use multivariate context carefully
sections.text: Several signals can move together because they share a common thermal, material or machine cause. Correlated channels are not independent confirmations of the same root cause. Compare their timing and physical relationships and avoid counting multiple derived values from one underlying sensor as separate evidence. More channels improve diagnosis only when they add distinct information.

chapters.applicability: General framework for thermoplastic moulded parts. Measurement conditioning and acceptance follow product/standard requirements.

sections.title: Dimensions can continue to change after ejection
sections.text: A moulded part can change dimensions after ejection as it cools, relaxes, absorbs moisture or responds to its storage and test environment. Before comparing measurements, define when and how the part is conditioned, which datums are used, how it is supported and which instrument or fixture measures it. Then distinguish immediate moulding shrinkage from later movement. A dimension without measurement time, condition and method is incomplete evidence. Look at direction and location as well as the reported value.

sections.title: Define the reference condition before comparing parts
sections.text: Specify time after moulding, temperature, humidity or conditioning state, measurement equipment, datum scheme and operator method. Without a common reference condition, apparent process variation may actually be measurement-timing or conditioning variation.

sections.title: Separate moulding shrinkage from later dimensional movement
sections.text: Mould-to-part dimensional difference immediately after moulding and subsequent dimensional change are related but not identical questions. Track the dimension through time when the product requirement depends on delayed conditioning or stabilisation.

sections.title: Use direction and location as evidence
sections.text: Flow direction, transverse direction, fibre orientation, wall transitions, inserts, ribs and cooling layout can create anisotropic or local dimensional behavior. Mapping which dimensions move, in what direction and at what time helps distinguish global scale change from local distortion.

sections.title: Check the measurement system and fixture influence
sections.text: Contact force, fixturing, datum repeatability, part temperature and operator technique can contribute meaningful variation, especially for flexible or thin parts. Confirm the measurement method is capable before attributing small dimensional shifts to the moulding process.

sections.title: Evidence that points beyond a process-only explanation
sections.text: Change the working diagnosis when the dimensional trend follows conditioning rather than process settings, differs by cavity or direction, disappears with improved measurement control, or persists after the suspected process variable is stabilised. The appropriate conclusion may be material-, tooling-, measurement- or product-design related instead of process-only.

sections.title: Build a dimensional time profile
sections.text: When a dimension evolves after moulding, measure it at defined intervals under controlled conditions rather than choosing one convenient time. The resulting profile can show rapid thermal contraction followed by slower material or moisture-related change. This helps distinguish a process change from a difference in when the part happened to be measured.

sections.title: Define datum strategy before analysing small changes
sections.text: A component can appear to change dimension because the measurement datum or fixturing changes as the part distorts. Use a repeatable datum system that reflects the product requirement, and record whether the measurement is size, position, form or a derived relationship. For flexible parts, measurement force and support can be part of the observed variation.

sections.title: Separate cavity bias from common drift
sections.text: If one cavity is consistently offset while all cavities move together over time, there may be both a cavity-specific effect and a shared thermal or material effect. Analyse those components separately. Pooling them into one average can hide a persistent tooling difference and exaggerate apparent random process variation.

sections.title: Worked example (hypothetical): distinguish a measurement-time change from a process change
sections.text:
A team reports that a critical dimension has shifted, but samples were measured at different times after moulding and with different support. Before changing the process, make the comparison conditions explicit. Record the time after ejection, conditioning environment, measurement instrument, datum, fixture or support, operator method and cavity for every sample. Follow the product and material requirements for the actual conditioning conditions.

Now separate the questions. Does the dimension change within the same part population as time passes? Do all cavities move in a similar direction, or does one cavity remain offset? Does the result change when the same measurement method and datum are applied consistently? These patterns help distinguish common post-mould movement, cavity bias and measurement influence. They do not prove the physical mechanism without further evidence.

A useful study plan assigns stable sample identities and a defined measurement schedule chosen by the applicable product or material requirement. It measures the required dimensions in relevant directions and keeps parts under comparable conditions. The record should distinguish a dimension taken soon after moulding from one taken after the specified conditioning period; combining them into one average can conceal the difference being investigated.

If the dimension changes over time while the process state is stable, the team should evaluate post-mould thermal or material effects within the applicable evidence. If only one cavity differs under the same measurement conditions, retain that cavity identity and examine local tooling or process evidence. If the apparent shift disappears when the fixture or datum is controlled, the measurement system contributed to the result. Several mechanisms can coexist, so the investigation should preserve more than one explanation when needed.

The example does not prescribe an interval, environment or acceptance limit. Those belong to the governing product and material requirements. Its purpose is to show why a dimensional value is incomplete without the conditions under which it was obtained.

A simple results table can keep these comparisons honest: sample identity, cavity, dimension and direction, datum, measurement method, time after ejection, conditioning state, and result. Use the same table for each observation point so that a missing value is visible. If a part is flexible, record its support and measurement force where relevant; otherwise a fixture difference can look like a material or process change. Keep the raw measurements as well as a summary. An average can describe a group, but it can also hide a cavity that remains consistently different.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: General reinforced-thermoplastic behavior. Magnitude and property data are grade- and geometry-specific.

sections.title: Orientation creates anisotropy
sections.text: Anisotropy means a material’s measured response depends on direction. In a short-fibre moulding compound, flow can align fibres, so a tensile result along the dominant direction may differ from one across it. The pattern is created locally as material moves around gates, ribs, bosses and holes, then freezes at different rates through the wall. Treat direction as part of every test result: state specimen location, flow direction and loading direction.

sections.title: Orientation connects flow history to directional properties
sections.text: The gate establishes an initial flow field, but local geometry changes it. Fibres rotate, bend, break or reorient as the melt accelerates, turns, splits and rejoins. Near a wall, shear often produces a layer with fibres aligned more parallel to flow; the core can have a different, sometimes more transverse distribution. That is a useful conceptual model, not a fixed number of layers. The part’s mechanical and dimensional response follows the spatial distribution, not simply the nominal fibre percentage.

sections.title: Infer carefully and measure where it matters
sections.text: A flow-path sketch and part geometry can identify likely high-risk regions, but they cannot prove the fibre orientation in a production part. Validate the directions that carry load or control fit using suitable specimens, microscopy, tomography or a calibrated simulation. Keep sample location and orientation traceable. If a result disagrees with the flow hypothesis, revisit the gate, geometry, process history and measurement method instead of forcing the interpretation.

sections.title: Skin-core structure can create competing directions
sections.text: The material next to a cooled mould wall experiences a different velocity and cooling history from the central flow. This can create a skin/core orientation profile, and the core response may differ from the surface. The profile can vary with wall thickness, material, gate, flow rate and thermal boundary conditions. A surface observation alone cannot establish the through-thickness structure. Consider cross-sections or a validated model when the component risk depends on this gradient.

sections.title: Geometry changes can redirect orientation
sections.text: Ribs, bosses, corners, holes and thickness transitions redirect flow and change local fibre alignment. These features can create stress concentrations at the same locations where orientation and shrinkage differ. Draw the flow paths around each feature, identify where fronts split and reunite, then connect the expected directions to the component’s load case. A gate relocation or geometry change can alter the entire local distribution, so compare the part after any approved change.

sections.title: Validate simulations against physical evidence
sections.text: A simulation predicts orientation from its material model, mesh, boundary conditions and process inputs. Its result is conditional on those assumptions and should not be presented as a direct measurement. Check the exact grade data, gate and cooling representation, and whether predicted flow and orientation agree with physical observations. Use sectioning, microscopy or micro-CT where justified, and record the sampled region. A validated model can help compare design options; it does not eliminate product testing.

sections.title: Worked example (hypothetical): map directions before explaining a result
sections.text: A hypothetical reinforced bracket cracks along one rib after assembly. First draw the local flow direction and expected fibre directions at the rib root, weld front and gate. Then compare the crack plane with those directions, inspect the fractured surface and confirm the material and conditioning. If the evidence supports an orientation-related weakness, a design or material review may be warranted; if it does not, investigate weld quality, stress concentration, process history and assembly load. The example is a reasoning exercise, not a diagnosis of a real component.

sections.title: Orientation is a spatial field, not one arrow
sections.text: For engineering use, orientation is better represented as a distribution of fibre directions at each location. A second-order orientation tensor, often written as an average of direction-vector products, compresses that distribution into a mathematical summary. It can represent preferred alignment and spread, but it does not retain every detail of fibre length, clustering or local damage. An orientation tensor is not a single fibre direction and cannot, by itself, prove strength. Interpret it with the constitutive model and the measurement or simulation method that produced it.

sections.title: What micro-CT and simulation can contribute
sections.text: Micro-computed tomography can reconstruct fibre geometry in a small sampled volume and estimate local orientation, subject to resolution, segmentation and sample-preparation limits. Simulation can estimate a larger field across the part, subject to the material model, mesh and process inputs. The methods answer different questions and have different uncertainties. Cross-check them where possible: sample a region the model predicts to be critical, then compare the measured and predicted distributions. Neither method substitutes for testing the component’s required performance.

sections.title: Plan measurements in the directions that matter
sections.text: Start with the component load case and identify locations where failure, fit or distortion matters. Select specimens or extracted regions that preserve relevant flow and through-thickness direction; record gate distance and orientation. Measure the property tied to the product requirement rather than collecting a generic tensile value. Use enough locations to expose gradients and cavity differences. The plan should state what result would change the design decision and what uncertainty remains.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Conceptual guidance only. High-rate processing must remain within the actual machine, mould, material and hot-runner limits.

sections.title: Machine capability matters
sections.text: A thin-wall feature creates a short time and pressure path for the melt to reach the end of the cavity before cooling raises resistance. Success depends on the exact material, wall geometry, gate design, venting, machine response and mould thermal condition. A label such as “thin-wall” does not prescribe a high-speed setting. Define the feature and quality requirement, verify what the machine can actually deliver, and build a bounded process study with the approved equipment and supplier guidance.

sections.title: Avoid universal high-speed rules
sections.text: Required rate depends on polymer rheology, geometry, gate and thermal condition. Establish it experimentally within supplier and equipment limits.

sections.title: Thin sections compress the available process window
sections.text: As flow paths become thinner relative to their length, pressure demand, cooling rate and sensitivity to small changes can increase. The process may have less tolerance for material, thermal, venting and machine-delivery variation. This makes measurement of actual machine response and mould behaviour especially important.

sections.title: Machine capability must be demonstrated, not assumed
sections.text: A high commanded velocity or pressure limit does not prove the machine can deliver the required profile through the actual mould. Review achievable velocity, acceleration, pressure response, transfer repeatability, shot utilisation and relevant equipment limits with the real system. Thin-wall processing should not be reduced to a generic instruction to run faster or hotter.

sections.title: Worked example (hypothetical): a thin-wall cavity does not fill consistently
sections.text:
A thin-wall part fills completely in some cycles and remains short in others. The controller's requested velocity profile looks unchanged. That observation does not prove the machine delivered the same motion, and the symptom does not by itself identify the machine as the limit.

First preserve the cavity and time pattern. If one cavity is consistently different, investigate the local flow path, gate, venting and thermal evidence alongside machine response. If all cavities change together, review common upstream conditions such as material preparation, machine delivery and mould state. Compare equivalent process states so that warm-up or an interruption is not confused with a cavity imbalance.

Then separate command from achieved behaviour. Review actual filling motion, acceleration or response where the controller makes it available, the transfer event, shot-use evidence and pressure demand. A nominal pressure rating or a high requested rate cannot alone demonstrate capability through this specific mould. Also preserve the actual material identity and the conditions required by its supplier. No single machine specification resolves a mismatch between the requested profile and the observed fill.

Choose a study that can distinguish the leading explanations without exceeding approved machine, mould, hot-runner, material or site limits. A controlled fill progression may help describe where the flow front stops; cavity-resolved part observations help show whether the effect is local or shared. Tooling changes require stronger evidence than a single unstable run. Do not convert the example into a universal instruction to run faster or hotter.

A sound report says what the machine was asked to do, what response was observed, which cavities were affected, and what the part showed. It also states whether the evidence supports a capability limit, a local restriction, a thermal difference or an unresolved combination.

When comparing two cycles, preserve both the requested profile and the achieved response rather than recording only the controller setting. Also keep the mould and material context with the trace: cavity, gate path, vent condition, thermal state and relevant preparation. If the machine response differs before the flow reaches the thin region, the study should examine delivery and control behavior. If the response is repeatable but one cavity remains different, local flow-path evidence deserves attention. These observations help decide which specialist or measurement is needed next; they do not authorize a faster profile or a tooling change.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: General balance methodology. Cavity layout, runner system and acceptance criteria are mould-specific.

sections.title: Equal nominal geometry does not guarantee equal cavity behavior
sections.text: In a multi-cavity mould, each cavity shares the machine but may see a different flow, thermal and mechanical history. Runner length, gate dimensions, venting, cooling balance, cavity geometry and wear can create repeatable cavity-to-cavity differences. Label measurements by cavity rather than averaging them away. Compare at equivalent cycle states to separate a stable imbalance from a drifting process. Tooling changes need evidence because a process compensation may improve one cavity while moving another away from its requirement.

sections.title: Preserve cavity identity in the data
sections.text: Record part mass, critical dimensions, defects and useful process signals by cavity. Pooling all parts into one average can hide one biased or unstable cavity and can make a balanced process appear noisier than it really is.

sections.title: Separate static imbalance from dynamic instability
sections.text: A cavity that is consistently heavier or fills earlier suggests a repeatable bias; a cavity that alternates or drifts suggests a different mechanism. Review both cavity means and time behavior before deciding whether the problem is runner/gate balance, thermal behavior, venting, measurement or another cause.

sections.title: Compare at equivalent process states
sections.text: Balance studies should control material condition, machine warm-up, mould thermal state, transfer method and sampling sequence. Otherwise time drift can be mistaken for cavity difference, particularly when cavities are measured in a fixed order.

sections.title: Tooling changes need stronger evidence than process compensation
sections.text: Changing a gate, runner or cavity feature can permanently alter the mould. Before modifying steel, demonstrate that the observed imbalance is repeatable, cavity-specific and not adequately explained by measurement, contamination, vent condition, thermal imbalance or process instability.

sections.title: When a cavity-balance explanation no longer fits
sections.text: Reconsider a cavity-balance diagnosis when the bias changes sides with measurement order, disappears after thermal stabilisation or cleaning, follows a material or machine change, or is not repeatable across runs. Escalate unresolved imbalance with cavity-resolved evidence instead of masking it with a global setting change.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: Source-first framework only. Processing windows, drying, residence and equipment requirements are grade-specific.

sections.title: Use grade documents as controlling evidence
sections.text: A high-temperature polymer family name is not enough to establish a processing route. Exact grades can differ in melt transitions, viscosity, reinforcement, moisture sensitivity and recommended handling. Read the supplier’s current technical datasheet, processing guide and safety information for the exact grade and form. Check revision dates, stated test methods and whether the document addresses the machine or mould condition you need. Treat this chapter’s examples as questions to ask, never as production settings.

sections.title: High temperature increases the importance of system limits
sections.text: A grade processed at elevated temperature places demands on the barrel, screw, seals, nozzle, hot runner, mould, temperature-control unit, sensors and ventilation system. Compatibility and safe operating limits must be checked across that full system. A machine displaying a temperature setpoint does not establish that every component can safely reach or sustain it. Confirm the equipment manual, risk assessment, material supplier instructions and qualified site review before any trial.

sections.title: Worked example (hypothetical): review a proposed material change
sections.text: A hypothetical engineer proposes replacing a standard engineering thermoplastic with a higher-temperature grade because a component softened in service. The review first confirms the actual failure temperature, load, duration, environment and conditioning. It then compares exact-grade evidence, mouldability, shrinkage, anisotropy, assembly and ageing. The candidate may solve one service limitation while creating new tooling, dimensional or safety constraints. The decision is a controlled engineering qualification, not a swap based on a family label.

sections.title: A high-performance grade is a complete system question
sections.text: Before a material trial, check whether the machine and screw are suitable, temperature zones and sensors are rated, the hot runner is compatible, the mould can tolerate the thermal cycle, and local extraction and handling arrangements are adequate. Review wear, corrosion, residence history and cleaning requirements for the specific polymer. A material supplier can define grade-specific requirements, but the equipment owner and qualified personnel must authorize the setup and operation.

sections.title: Follow the material’s entire thermal history
sections.text: High melt temperatures can make waiting time and stagnant regions consequential. Track startup, interruptions, purge and recovery using the supplier’s procedures; do not extrapolate a general residence-time rule from another polymer. A defect that appears after a pause may point to material history, but it still needs evidence from colour, appearance, cavity pattern and process timeline. Avoid repeated purge or temperature actions until the approved procedure and material safety limits are known.

sections.title: Read each supplier document for the question it answers
sections.text: A datasheet provides selected properties under stated tests; a processing guide gives supplier recommendations for a grade and equipment class; a safety data sheet describes hazards and handling; a machine or hot-runner manual controls equipment use. One document does not replace the others. Record the exact revision and unresolved questions. Where documents conflict or omit a critical limit, stop the transfer decision and ask the supplier or qualified engineer.

chapters.reviewBoundary: Technical-review draft. Use the actual material, machine, mould, hot-runner and site documentation before applying production changes.

chapters.applicability: General advanced diagnostic method; production and safety decisions remain governed by site authority.

sections.title: Several mechanisms can fit the same symptom
sections.text: When the basic diagnostic loop leaves several plausible causes, treat the investigation as a system problem. Material history, flow resistance, temperature, tool condition, machine response and measurement error may interact. List mechanisms separately and note where they could produce similar evidence. The goal is not to name the most familiar cause but to identify which evidence can distinguish the alternatives safely.

sections.title: Create competing hypotheses with predicted observations
sections.text: For each hypothesis, write its causal path, expected affected population, timing, location and signal pattern. Include at least one observation that would weaken it. Keep predictions specific to the actual material, machine and mould, because a general rule may not hold for this setup. This makes uncertainty visible before new data arrives.

sections.title: Prioritise discriminating evidence
sections.text: Rank the next measurements by how much they could change the decision, how reliable they are and what risk they involve. A high-value measurement may be cavity-resolved, time-aligned or independent of the signal that first raised concern. Avoid collecting many correlated metrics that all reflect the same sensor or assumption.

sections.title: Beware of correlated signals and successful-but-wrong fixes
sections.text: Two signals can move together because they share a sensor, calculation or common upstream cause. Treating them as independent confirmation exaggerates confidence. A change can also suppress a symptom while leaving the initiating cause in place—for example, one effect may compensate for another. Check whether the fix remains effective across the affected population and whether it creates a new risk.

sections.title: Preserve an evidence ledger
sections.text: For each observation, record source, time, sample identity, method, units, conditions, uncertainty and the hypothesis it supports or challenges. Distinguish direct observation from interpretation and supplier guidance from local measurement. Retain contradictory evidence rather than discarding it. An evidence ledger lets another engineer reconstruct why the conclusion was reached.

sections.title: What should lower confidence in the leading hypothesis
sections.text: Confidence should fall when predicted evidence is absent, the pattern crosses an unexpected boundary, the measurement is unreliable, an alternative explains more observations, or the intervention changes several factors at once. Also lower confidence when a result comes from a different grade, geometry, sensor location or conditioning state. Revise the hypothesis explicitly instead of explaining away every contradiction.

sections.title: Build a causal timeline
sections.text: Align material batches, machine events, mould maintenance, alarms, environmental changes and part measurements on one timeline. Include when the condition began and when it was detected, since those may differ. Use source records rather than recollection where possible. The timeline narrows possible initiating events, but it remains a map of evidence and not a causal proof.

sections.title: Use population boundaries as experiments
sections.text: Compare affected and unaffected cavities, shifts, lots, time periods or part regions while controlling important differences. A boundary can reveal whether the cause is shared or local. Check that labels, sampling and measurement methods are consistent; otherwise the apparent boundary may be an artifact. When possible, collect paired observations under the same conditions.

sections.title: Beware compensating mechanisms
sections.text: A process can appear stable because two changes offset one another. For example, a higher flow resistance and a different temperature history might produce a similar fill time while changing pressure demand or part structure. A single output can hide this interaction. Track mechanism-relevant signals and product characteristics together, and avoid declaring recovery from one metric alone.

sections.title: Define the stopping rule for investigation
sections.text: Before continuing, state what evidence would be sufficient for containment, correction, release or a request for outside expertise. Include the level of residual risk that requires escalation and who has authority to accept it. Stop when the evidence supports the permitted decision, not when every uncertainty has disappeared. Keep unresolved questions visible in the handover.

sections.title: Independent review is valuable when the evidence is ambiguous
sections.text: A second reviewer is especially useful when the leading explanation is consequential, the evidence is contradictory, or the proposed correction affects safety, tooling or product qualification. Provide the reviewer with the actual records, assumptions, uncertainty and alternative hypotheses. This chapter’s internal review does not substitute for an independent materials, process, tooling or product specialist.

sections.title: Rank hypotheses by evidence, consequence and testability
sections.text: A practical ranking considers how well each hypothesis explains the observations, the consequence if it is wrong, and whether a safe test can discriminate it. Do not rank by familiarity alone. Keep the ranking provisional and update it as evidence changes. High-consequence possibilities may need containment even when they are not the most likely explanation.

sections.title: Distinguish containment, correction and root-cause evidence
sections.text: Containment limits exposure while the cause is uncertain. A correction restores an acceptable condition under a defined scope. Root-cause evidence explains why the failure occurred and why the control failed to prevent or detect it. These are different outcomes and may require different evidence. Do not present a temporary containment or a successful adjustment as a complete corrective action.

sections.title: Use contradictions as valuable data
sections.text: When a trace suggests one mechanism and the part result suggests another, check alignment, timing, calibration, cavity identity and sample conditioning. The conflict may expose a hidden process stage or measurement problem. Preserve both results and ask what model assumption connects them. Do not discard the measurement that fails to fit the preferred explanation.

sections.title: Worked example (hypothetical): choose the next measurement when evidence conflicts
sections.text: In a hypothetical multi-cavity case, machine pressure is stable, but one cavity shows intermittent weight loss and a downstream dimension shifts after conditioning. The team separates the machine signal’s location from the cavity response, checks sensor and measurement repeatability, and compares material lot and cooling conditions. They select a cavity-specific measurement that can test a local-flow explanation against a later dimensional-change explanation. No single result proves the cause; the example shows how to pick the next question and retain uncertainty.
